body.objective: Students will be able to build trust and focus with ensemble games.
body.iCan: I can build trust and focus with ensemble games.
successCriteria: I can concentrate and stay focused in a group activity

body.hook: On stage, actors have to trust each other completely. If your scene partner forgets a line, you need to catch them. If someone falls in a scene, you need to know the group has their back. Drama starts not with acting, but with trust and focus.

study.title: Building the Ensemble
study.question: How do trust and focus help a group create drama?
study.passage:
Ground rules: respect, safety, no touching without consent and instruction, and "pass" is always an option.
Warm-up, Pass the clap (5 minutes): In a circle, pass a clap from person to person, making eye contact. Then speed up, reverse direction, and send two claps at once.
Game 1, Count to 20 (5 minutes): The group counts to 20 one person at a time, with no set order. If two people speak at once, start again. Eyes closed for the second round.
Game 2, Mirror (8 minutes): In pairs, one leads slow movements and the other mirrors exactly. Switch leaders. Then try with no leader, both following each other.
Game 3, Guided walk (10 minutes): One partner closes their eyes (or uses a blindfold if comfortable). The other guides them around the room with gentle verbal directions only. Switch. Side-coaching: "Guides, keep your partner safe. Walkers, notice how it feels to trust."
Debrief circle (5 minutes): How did it feel to trust? What helped? Where did focus slip?
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.

organizer: What I had to focus on
discussion: Why was Count to 20 hard at first?
What made the mirror activity work best?
How did it feel to be guided? To guide?

successCriteria: I can show emotions with facial expression
I can use gesture to communicate meaning without words

body.hook: Turn off the sound on a movie and you can still tell who is angry, who is scared and who is in love. Bodies and faces talk all the time. Actors learn to control that silent language on purpose.

vocabulary.definition: A movement of the body, hands or head that communicates meaning.

study.title: Silent Signals
study.question: How can the body and face communicate without words?
study.passage:
Activities (written for this lesson):
1. Emotion faces (5 minutes): In a circle, the leader calls an emotion: joy, fear, disgust, surprise, anger, sadness. Everyone shows it on the face only, then freezes. Look around: how do different people show the same feeling?
2. Scale it up (5 minutes): Show "happy" at level 1 (barely), 5 (clearly) and 10 (huge). Discuss which level a theatre audience at the back of the room could read.
3. Gesture dictionary (10 minutes): In small groups, find gestures for: come here, go away, I don't know, I'm thinking, stop, I'm cold, I'm tired, I won. Perform them for another group to guess.
4. Silent conversation (15 minutes): In pairs, have a 30-second conversation using only face and gesture. Situations: returning a borrowed item that broke; asking someone to dance; finding out you won a prize. The audience explains what happened.
Side-coaching: "Exaggerate so the back row can see." "Hold your freeze."

body.objective: Students will be able to create a mime sequence.
body.iCan: I can create a mime sequence.
successCriteria: I can create believable imaginary objects through mime
I can plan a mime sequence with a beginning, middle and end
I can perform a mime that an audience understands
body.hook: The French mime artist Marcel Marceau performed for over 60 years without saying a word on stage. His character Bip, with a white face and a striped shirt, could climb invisible stairs, walk against the wind and catch butterflies. Mime makes the invisible visible.

vocabulary.definition: Acting without words, using the body to show actions, objects and feelings.
An object that isn't there but is shown through mime.

Where the performer looks, which tells the audience where things are.

study.title: Making the Invisible Visible
study.question: How can mime show objects, actions and stories without words?
study.passage:
Activities (written for this lesson):
1. Mime technique (15 minutes):
The wall: Place flat hands on an invisible wall. Keep them at the same spot as you move your body. Add the "click" when hands arrive.
Weight: Pick up an imaginary feather, then a heavy suitcase. Bend the knees, strain the face and change your walk.
Shape and size: Pass an imaginary ball around the circle. It must stay the same size; then the leader changes it into something else.
2. Plan (10 minutes): In groups of three, plan a 60-second mime with a beginning (where are we, who are we), a middle (a problem) and an end (how it's solved or what changes). Ideas: a picnic interrupted by rain; a lost puppy in a busy street; moving into a new home. Use at least three imaginary objects.
3. Rehearse and perform (20 minutes): Rehearse, then perform. The audience retells the story afterward. Did they see the same objects you imagined?
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; Marcel Marceau facts are widely documented.
steps: Practise the wall, weight and shape techniques
Plan a 60-second mime with a beginning, middle and end
Include at least three imaginary objects
Perform and hear the audience retell it
discussion: Which imaginary object was most believable? Why?
